blocks.text: 1. Naive RAG
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447581975-963564001.png

Guardrails closed out the Prompt Engineering for RAG module, wrapping up how prompts control a RAG assistant's behavior. Naive RAG, the simplest retrieve then generate pipeline, opens the Advanced RAG module by naming the baseline every later pattern improves on.
It embeds the query, retrieves the top chunks, stuffs them into the prompt, and generates an answer, a four step pipeline.
2. The Four Stage Pipeline
Naive RAG runs exactly four stages in sequence: embed the query, retrieve the top k chunks by similarity, insert those chunks into the prompt, and generate the final answer.
No stage loops back to an earlier one, and no stage checks the output of the previous stage before continuing.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Stage","What happens"],"rows":[["Embed query","Query text is converted into a vector"],["Retrieve","Top k chunks by similarity are fetched"],["Insert","Retrieved chunks are placed into the prompt"],["Generate","The model produces the final answer"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Why Naive Means Simple Not Wrong
Naive describes the absence of extra correction or planning steps, not a judgment of quality.
A well tuned naive pipeline still handles a large share of real questions well.
4. Single Retrieval Pass Only
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447581975-371534698.png
The pipeline retrieves exactly once and never re-queries based on what it generates.
There is no opportunity to notice or correct a poor initial retrieval.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Once the top k chunks are retrieved, naive RAG has no mechanism to go back and retrieve again, even if the generated answer later reveals the retrieved chunks were the wrong ones.

blocks.text: 5. No Grading Of The Retrieved Chunks

blocks.alt: No Grading Of The Retrieved Chunks
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447581975-616594697.png
Naive RAG trusts every retrieved chunk equally, with no relevance check like the top-k selection covered in Re-Ranking.
An irrelevant chunk gets passed to the model just like a relevant one.
6. Where Naive RAG Breaks Down
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447581975-879225152.png
Questions needing several chained facts, or a query poorly matched to the actual chunk wording, expose the pipeline's limits.
This is the same multi-hop retrieval challenge, gathering facts across several documents, covered in Retrieval.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Question type","Naive RAG behavior"],"rows":[["Single fact, well matched wording","Typically retrieves and answers correctly"],["Multi-hop or poorly matched wording","Often retrieves incomplete or irrelevant chunks"]]}

blocks.text: 7. Naive RAG As The Baseline
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447719517-78069949.png
Every more advanced pattern covered later in this module adds a specific correction on top of this same four stage pipeline.
Naive RAG is the reference point every improvement is measured against.
8. Cost And Latency Advantage
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447719519-214525186.png
As with reasoning token cost, covered in Chain Of Thought, one retrieval call and one generation call means the lowest possible latency and cost.
Every added correction step in later patterns adds its own cost.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Because naive RAG makes exactly one retrieval call and one generation call, it remains the fastest and cheapest pattern in this module, a real advantage for simple, high volume workloads.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Naive RAG Is The Right Choice

blocks.alt: Recognizing When Naive RAG Is The Right Choice
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447719519-555217703.png
Simple, well matched single fact questions suit naive RAG well.
Complex, multi-step questions, by contrast, need one of the corrective patterns covered next.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates the four stage naive RAG pipeline as a minimal function chain.

code.content:
def embed(text):
    # the four stage pipeline
    return [len(word) for word in text.split()][:8]

def retrieve(query_vector, chunks, top_k=2):
    scored = sorted(chunks, key=lambda c: abs(sum(embed(c)) - sum(query_vector)))
    return scored[:top_k]

def build_prompt(chunks, query):
    context = "\n".join(f"- {c}" for c in chunks)
    return f"Context:\n{context}\n\nQuestion: {query}\nAnswer:"

def generate(prompt):
    # simulated generation step
    return "Simulated answer grounded in the retrieved context above."

chunks = [
    "The Falcon plan costs twenty dollars per month.",
    "Refunds are processed within five business days.",
    "Support is available on weekdays only.",
]
query = "How much does the Falcon plan cost?"

query_vector = embed(query)
top_chunks = retrieve(query_vector, chunks)
prompt = build_prompt(top_chunks, query)
answer = generate(prompt)

print("Naive RAG pipeline:")
print("Retrieved chunks:", top_chunks)
print("Prompt:\n", prompt)
print("Answer:", answer)

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows the pipeline retrieving once, building one prompt, and generating one answer with no loop back to retrieval, naive RAG's defining limitation.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Assuming naive RAG is always inferior rather than checking if it already meets the actual need.
Blaming the generation model when a poor answer actually traces back to poor retrieval.
Adding correction steps to every query even when the workload is simple and well matched.
Forgetting that naive RAG never re-queries, so a bad first retrieval cannot self-correct.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Naive RAG is the simplest pipeline: embed the query, retrieve, insert into the prompt, generate.
Naive describes the absence of extra correction or planning steps, not necessarily low quality.
The pipeline retrieves exactly once and never re-queries based on what it generates.
No relevance grading means an irrelevant chunk is treated the same as a relevant one.
Multi-hop questions or poorly matched query wording expose the pipeline's real limits.
Every more advanced pattern in this module adds a specific correction on top of this baseline.
One retrieval and one generation call give naive RAG the lowest possible latency and cost.
Next up: Advanced RAG, covering the general shift from this single pass pipeline toward added correction stages.
